This calculator instantly converts tire size notation into the actual diameter and circumference of your tire.

intro: A tire size like **205/55 R16** hides the one number that actually matters when you change wheels: the **overall diameter**. Get it wrong and your speedometer lies, your odometer drifts, and the new tire may rub the bodywork. This calculator turns the three-part code into the real diameter, circumference, and revolutions per kilometer in one step.
keyTakeaway: Overall diameter = **(rim in inches × 25.4) + 2 × (width × aspect ÷ 100)**, in millimeters. When switching sizes, keep the new diameter within **±3%** of the original — beyond that, your speedometer reading and gearing change noticeably.

explanation:
## Reading the tire code

A size like **205/55 R16** packs three measurements:

- **205** — tread width in millimeters (measured from sidewall to sidewall at the widest point, not the contact patch width, which is narrower).
- **55** — aspect ratio: the sidewall height is 55% of the tread width (205 × 0.55 ≈ 113 mm per sidewall).
- **R16** — radial construction on a 16-inch rim diameter.

The letter before the rim size matters too: **P** (passenger car), **LT** (light truck), or no letter (Euro metric) indicate load standards that affect maximum pressure and load index — but not the diameter calculation itself.

## How the diameter is calculated

The sidewall sits on **both** the top and bottom of the rim, so it counts twice. Because the rim is given in inches and everything else in millimeters, a unit conversion is required first:

```
Diameter (mm) = (rim_inches × 25.4) + 2 × (width_mm × aspect ÷ 100)
```

**For 205/55 R16:**

| Step | Operation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Rim in mm | 16 × 25.4 | 406.4 mm |
| One sidewall | 205 × 0.55 | 112.75 mm |
| Both sidewalls | 112.75 × 2 | 225.5 mm |
| **Total diameter** | 406.4 + 225.5 | **631.9 mm** |

Circumference = π × 631.9 ≈ **1,985 mm** (~1.985 m per wheel revolution). At 100 km/h the wheel rotates roughly 840 times per minute — the figure your speedometer and odometer are calibrated to.

## Why the ±3% rule exists

Your speedometer is calibrated to the factory tire's circumference. Fit a **larger** diameter and the wheel completes fewer revolutions per kilometer, so the speedometer reads **slower than actual speed** (and the odometer under-counts mileage). A **smaller** diameter does the opposite — your speedo reads high and you may be driving slower than you think on the highway.

Staying within **±3%** keeps errors small enough that speedometer accuracy, ABS sensor thresholds, traction control calibration, and transmission shift points all remain close to factory spec. Beyond that range, some jurisdictions require recalibration, and warranty claims on drivetrain components can be affected.

## Worked example: plus-sizing

Factory size **195/65 R15** → diameter ≈ 635 mm. Moving to 16-inch wheels, a **205/55 R16** gives ≈ 632 mm — only ~0.5% smaller, comfortably within ±3%. This is a textbook *plus-one* fitment: rim diameter increases by one inch, sidewall height drops to compensate, and overall diameter stays nearly identical. The benefit is a wider contact patch and stiffer sidewall for better cornering response; the trade-off is a firmer ride and typically higher tire cost.

## What this calculator does NOT include

- **Load index and speed rating** — a 205/55 R16 91V and a 205/55 R16 94H have identical diameters but different load capacities. Never downgrade these values without checking your vehicle's door-jamb placard.
- **Actual inflated vs. loaded diameter** — the formula gives the nominal unloaded diameter. Under the vehicle's weight, the tire deflects; the loaded radius is smaller. Engineers use loaded radius for suspension geometry, not this figure.
- **Section width vs. mount width** — tread width (205 mm) is the nominal value at the recommended rim width. On a narrower rim the tire "pinches" slightly narrower; on a wider rim it spreads. This doesn't change the diameter meaningfully but affects handling balance.
- **Wheel well clearance** — a larger diameter needs physical space. Always verify clearance at full steering lock and full suspension compression before purchasing.

## Common mistakes

**Confusing width with contact patch.** The 205 mm is the tire's widest cross-section, not how much rubber touches the road. The actual contact patch is roughly the size of your hand.

**Forgetting the ×2 for sidewalls.** One of the most frequent manual calculation errors — adding only one sidewall instead of two gives a diameter ~113 mm too small.

**Mixing up aspect ratio as a fixed number.** A 55-series on a wide tire is a much taller sidewall than a 55-series on a narrow one: 285/55 R20 has a 157 mm sidewall vs. 113 mm for 205/55 R16. The ratio is always relative to its own width.

**Assuming all R16 tires are interchangeable.** Two tires can share a rim size and be completely different in overall diameter. A 215/70 R16 (≈723 mm) and a 205/55 R16 (≈632 mm) both fit a 16-inch rim but differ by nearly 9 cm in diameter — a 14% difference.

## Quick reference: common diameters

| Size | Diameter | Circumference |
|---|---|---|
| 185/65 R15 | 625 mm | 1,963 mm |
| 195/65 R15 | 635 mm | 1,994 mm |
| 205/55 R16 | 632 mm | 1,985 mm |
| 225/45 R17 | 632 mm | 1,985 mm |
| 235/45 R18 | 657 mm | 2,064 mm |

Note how very different sizes can land on nearly identical diameters — exactly why matching overall diameter, not just rim size, is the correct approach when changing wheels.

faq.q: What does tire aspect ratio mean?
faq.a: Aspect ratio is the sidewall height as a percentage of tire width. A lower number (40%) means a flatter, sportier tire. A higher number (65%) means a taller sidewall with better comfort.
Rim diameter is the size of your wheel measured in inches. Common sizes are 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, and 20 inches. It's the third number in your tire size code (e.g., R16 = 16-inch rim).

faq.q: Can I use a different tire size?
faq.a: You can change tire sizes, but the new tire's overall diameter should be within 3% of the original. Larger deviations affect speedometer accuracy, fuel economy, and handling.

faq.q: How does tire size affect speedometer accuracy?
faq.a: Larger tires complete fewer rotations per mile, so your speedometer reads slower than you're actually going. Smaller tires have the opposite effect. Use this calculator to verify your speedometer accuracy.

faq.q: What's the difference between low-profile and high-profile tires?
faq.a: Low-profile tires have lower aspect ratios (under 50%), offering better handling and sportier feel. High-profile tires (over 60%) provide better comfort and smoother rides.
